questions.question_text: Which $12$-counter bag gives $P(\text{pink})=\frac{1}{3}$, with all remaining counters grey?

options.why: Used the denominator as the pink count instead of finding one-third of 12.
Assigned the complementary two-thirds to pink instead of one-third.

questions.question_text:
A spinner has $15$ equal sectors.
Which design makes $P(\text{diamond})=\frac{2}{5}$?

options.why: Used the numerator as the sector count without scaling the fraction to fifteenths.
Used the complementary three-fifths of the spinner for diamonds.

questions.question_text:
A bag contains only teal and gold counters.
Teal must be four times as likely as gold.
Which $10$-counter design works?

options.why: Read four times as likely as a count of four instead of a four-to-one ratio.
Made teal only one-and-a-half times as likely instead of four times.

questions.solution_text:
$\text{teal}:\text{gold}=4:1$
There are $5$ parts, each worth $2$ counters.
Use $8$ teal and $2$ gold.

questions.question_text: What is the smallest equal-sector spinner for $P(R)=\frac{1}{2}$, $P(S)=\frac{1}{5}$ and $P(T)=\frac{3}{10}$?

options.why: Rounded one-half of five to two sectors, changing the required probability.
Found a valid scaled design but not the smallest equal-sector design requested.

questions.solution_text:
The smallest common denominator is $10$.
Use $5R,2S,3T$ sectors.

questions.question_text:
A bag has $3$ red, $6$ blue and $9$ white counters.
Which scaled design keeps the same probabilities using $12$ counters?

options.why: Changed the colour ratio instead of scaling every count by the same factor.
Redistributed counters toward equal counts instead of preserving the original ratio.

questions.solution_text:
$3:6:9=1:2:3$
Twelve counters give $2$ per ratio part.
Use $2,4,6$.

questions.question_text:
A $10$-sector spinner must give three outcomes probabilities $\frac{3}{10}$, $\frac{1}{4}$ and the remainder.
Can it be made with equal sectors?

options.text: No; one-quarter of $10$ is not a whole number of sectors.

options.why: Rounded one-quarter of ten down to two sectors, changing the required probability.
Used the denominator four as the sector count for the one-quarter outcome.

questions.solution_text:
$\frac{1}{4}\times10=2.5$
Equal sectors cannot be split, so the design is not possible with $10$ sectors.
